children: The number of people dead in catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet rose to nearly 770, as teams from China and India arrived in Nepal to help with rescue efforts for hydropower project workers trapped in tunnels by mud deposited by the deluge.

Scientists examining the causes of Wednesday's flood believe it was sparked by part of a glacier on a Nepalese mountain collapsing along with some of its bedrock, sending an avalanche of ice and rock into the valley below where it turned into a debris-laden flood.

Scientists are working on calculating the volume of ice and debris in the avalanche, as well as looking at whether any advance warning signs could have signaled that the glacier and its bedrock were in danger of detaching.
At least 752 people are dead in Nepal, authorities there said, while 2,500 people are missing, many of them pilgrims who were visiting lakes in the area that Hindus and Buddhists consider sacred.

About 900 of the missing are workers from more than a dozen hydropower projects in operation or under construction, most of which appear to have been largely destroyed. Nepal has sought technical assistance and equipment in its rescue efforts, with both its giant neighbors dispatching teams to assess damaged hydropower project tunnels.

In Tibet, 16 people are dead, according to Chinese state-run news reports, and around 550 are missing. More than 100 Nepalese, some 49 Indians and 18 Americans are among the 261 foreign nationals missing, according to Tibetan authorities.

In as statement Saturday night, the Isha Foundation, which had a number of pilgrim groups traveling in the Nepal-China border region, including 77 people who were at the Gyirong Port, said information on rescue operations at the Chinese border checkpoint had given "no encouraging indications of survivors at the immigration office area."

"The mix of debris and water rose very high, probably as high as 150 ft with immense force, completely wiping out the whole building complex," the spiritual group said. "This is an unimaginable calamity."
Video from the port area, as well as from other locations in Nepal, showed military personnel and rescue workers crawling across the mud to avoid getting bogged down in it.

Experts say this year's flood, as well as one in 2025 in the same region that was caused by a lake in Tibet that burst, point to the need for rapidly improving transboundary sharing of risk analysis of hazards such as avalanches and glacial lake bursts in the Himalayas, a challenging task.

China's embassy in Nepal in recent days has responded to some Nepalese media reports and social-media comments that asked whether China had failed to provide Nepal with a warning. China said the country makes every effort to monitor Himalayan terrain for risks and share the information with its neighbor.
But the task is complicated by the fact that risks are dispersed across the Himalayas, while a 2015 earthquake destabilized many rock masses on the southern slopes, the embassy said.
"Furthermore, image errors on steep slopes and high-precision monitoring over vast and complex terrain remain an international challenge," the embassy said.
Meanwhile, ice vanishing due to climate warming is steadily destabilizing mountainous regions like the Himalayas, scientists say.
Nepal's government has said the nature of the disaster took time to understand, catching both countries by surprise.
